 Japan's largest labor union to seek around 6% pay hike next spring
 KYODO NEWS 
 - Oct 22, 2026 - 19:38 
 All , Japan 
 TOKYO - Japan's largest labor union said Thursday it will demand a wage hike of around 6 percent, with a minimum of 5 percent, in next spring's annual labor-management negotiations amid prolonged inflation.
 Although the Japanese Trade Union Confederation, also known as Rengo, achieved its target of wage hikes of 5 percent or more for three consecutive years through the 2026 "shunto" wage talks and real wages turned positive, it noted that "only a small number of people feel their standard of living has improved."
 Given the rising cost of living, the union decided a further wage increase was necessary and set a new midpoint target of 6 percent in its basic policy for the 2027 wage talks.
 As in the 2026 wage talks, the union urged its member unions at small and medium-sized firms to target wage hikes of at least 6 percent to narrow the pay gap with large companies.
 Rengo President Tomoko Yoshino said at a press conference that setting a higher target of around 6 percent would be "one of the key strategies, if we aim for 5 percent or more (pay rise)."
 The target covers both base-pay increases and regular raises based on workers' seniority and years of service.
 Consumer spending remains sluggish amid uncertainty over whether wages will continue to rise, the union noted in its policy. It added that extending wage increases to small and medium-sized firms and ensuring sustained growth in real wages would contribute to economic stability and a virtuous cycle.
 To narrow disparities based on employment status, the union set a wage hike target of 7 percent for non-regular workers, such as contract and part-time employees.
 The union also said it will seek a minimum hourly wage of at least 1,350 yen ($8.60), up 50 yen from its target in the 2026 wage talks, regardless of employment status.
 As a new mid-term goal, Rengo said that it aims to raise overall wages by around 15 percent by 2030.
 Real wages per worker rose for the eighth straight month in August, according to a survey by the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare.
